response.text:
Seven companies controlled 50% of America's meat supply, and within six months of a book's publication, they lost half of their sales. 📉 What happened, and why did it change the industry forever? Let's dive in! (1/8)

Back in 1906, Upton Sinclair published "The Jungle," exposing shocking conditions in Chicago's slaughterhouses. The public was horrified, and the book flew off the shelves. 📚 (2/8)

At that time, just seven companies dominated 50% of the U.S. meat market. Sinclair's revelations were enough to send these giants into a tailspin, losing half their sales in just six months. 🏭 (3/8)

Faced with bankruptcy, the CEOs of these companies turned to President Teddy Roosevelt, pleading for government intervention to regain consumer trust. It was a pivotal moment in food regulation history. 🇺🇸 (4/8)

Roosevelt's response? The creation of the Food Safety Inspection Service (FSIS) in 1908, initially excluding private sales. This move marked the start of federal food safety regulations. 🛡️ (5/8)

This was a turning point in American consumer advocacy, echoing the spirit of Ralph Nader's later work. The public's mistrust of big business was growing, and so was the demand for transparency. 🔍 (6/8)

The legacy of "The Jungle"? A reminder of the power of literature to spark change and the enduring need for vigilance in our food systems. Want to learn more about this transformative era? (7/8)

Dig deeper into this fascinating history and the impact of consumer advocacy. Share your thoughts! #FoodHistory #ConsumerAdvocacy #TheJungle (8/8)
